identification.summary: Sima is a tentative campaign/cluster name given by researchers Claudio Guarnieri and Collin Anderson to a suspected Iran-origin spearphishing operation, based on the recurring strings "PCSima7" and "PCSima9" in the metadata of Word documents displayed when the primary malware agent runs [S1][S2]. Reported lures include a February 2016 message impersonating a Human Rights Watch official and linking to a real HRW report, and a March 2016 message impersonating US immigration [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Early 2016 (lures reported for February and March 2016) [S2]. Earlier activity not established in the sources reviewed.
identification.notes: Name is a researcher-assigned tentative label, not a vendor-tracked group with a Microsoft name. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID identified. The Black Hat paper treats Sima alongside Rocket Kitten, Infy and Operation Cleaver as separate clusters [S1]; do not merge their facts.

attribution.confidence: Guarnieri and Anderson assessed Iranian origin; Foreign Policy reported that the evidence for Iranian responsibility was circumstantial, though the researchers' case on tactics and tooling was considered strong [S2]. No state sponsor or government attribution identified.

sectors: Civil society and human rights (Iran-focused individuals)
targeting.notes: Iran-focused individuals and members of the Iranian diaspora were targeted using lures matched to their professional interests, e.g. HRW material on Iran and Afghan refugees [S2]. The group was reported to monitor targets and respond quickly to their perceived interests [S2].

capabilities.summary: Spearphishing with impersonation of real, professionally relevant individuals and organizations (a Human Rights Watch official, US immigration), real topical documents as bait, and links to malware hosted elsewhere [S2]. Malware binaries masqueraded as legitimate files using right-to-left override filenames [S2]. The primary malware agent displays Word documents containing the PCSima7/PCSima9 metadata strings [S1]. One dropper was reported to be clumsy, producing repeated pop-ups during installation [S2].

campaigns.name: Human Rights Watch impersonation lure
campaigns.summary: Iran-focused recipients received messages purporting to be from a senior HRW official, pointing to a real HRW report on Iran sending Afghan refugees to fight in Syria; the linked biography and article led to malware hosted elsewhere [S2].

campaigns.name: US immigration impersonation lure
campaigns.summary: A March 2016 email purporting to be from US immigration was attributed by the researchers to Sima [S2].

campaigns.name: Public disclosure at Black Hat USA
campaigns.summary: Guarnieri and Anderson published "Iran and the Soft War for Internet Dominance", naming Sima and describing its tradecraft [S1][S2].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed suspected Iran-origin operators; no sponsor established [S2].
diamond.capability: Impersonation spearphishing, RTLO-disguised binaries, primary malware agent with decoy Word documents [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Malware hosted on third-party sites linked from lures [S2]. No specific indicators gathered.
diamond.victim: Iran-focused individuals and diaspora members, including human rights-related contacts [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Researchers frame Iranian operations against dissidents and civil society within Iran's "soft war" concept [S1]. Specific tasking for Sima not established.
diamond.technology: Email, Windows endpoints executing disguised binaries and Word documents [S1][S2].

gaps: Could not open the Black Hat white paper, iranthreats.github.io, Malpedia, or Foreign Policy directly (fetch failed); details rely on search-result excerpts of these documents.
No sponsor, organizational affiliation, or government attribution identified.
Malware family names, hashes, C2 infrastructure and exact dates of first and last activity not obtained.
No reporting found after 2016; current activity status and any overlap with later Iranian clusters unknown.
Victim counts specific to Sima not established; scale figures in coverage appear to refer to the researchers' wider dataset or other malware.

Removed unverified claims (open mail relays, Persian-language lures, Visual Studio piracy-site indicator, 'most sophisticated' ranking) that search could not confirm; search excerpts instead describe Sima as having strong English-language social engineering. Malpedia lists Infy as a Sima synonym, which conflicts with the Black Hat paper's separate-cluster treatment and is unresolved.
